title: Streaming throughput collapse postmortem 2027-10-11
summary: On 2027-10-11 we had a P0 where a kernel-level regression combined with routing affinity bugs caused a subset of streaming sessions to stall, producing high tail latency and reconnect storms. Emergency routing fallback and a canary rollback restored baseline within ~50 minutes.
content:
Overview:
At ~09:23 UTC on 2027-10-11 monitoring alerted to a sharp fall in streaming throughput for the hosted inference API. Approximately 18% of streaming sessions experienced severe stalls: p99 tail latency rose above 15s, streaming frames were fragmented or never delivered, and many clients issued reconnects. The outage was mitigated to minimal customer impact by 10:10 UTC after emergency routing fallback and rollback of a kernel canary.

Scope and impact:
- Peak affected sessions: ~12k active streaming sessions (est.).
- Services impacted: streaming responses (chat widgets, realtime websockets, webhook-driven pipelines).
- Business impact: transient degraded UX and increased error rates. No sustained billing discrepancies found.

How we detected it:
- stream.sessions.throughput_pct_drop alert triggered at 09:23 UTC (threshold: 10% sustained drop across regional pools).
- Dashboards showed asymmetric distribution of streams: pool-7 had elevated write latency and CPU sys time.
- Pager notified SRE on-call (Lucas). Triage started within 4 minutes.

Detailed timeline (abridged):
- 09:12 UTC: infra initiated a rolling kernel/libnv package update targeting gpu-serving clusters (canary nodes first). (infra-job-321)
- 09:20 UTC: small number of canary nodes began showing increased socket write latency on internal metrics.
- 09:23 UTC: global streaming throughput alert fires; error rates start to tick up.
- 09:27 UTC: on-call increased logging and examined routing table; observed many long-lived affinity entries pointing to canaried nodes.
- 09:30 UTC: attempted short-term ingress concurrency bump and worker restarts on pool-7; minimal effect.
- 09:35 UTC: discovered health-check evaluation was using mean latency and did not invalidate affinity entries on p95/p99 degradation.
- 09:42 UTC: enabled emergency routing fallback policy (prefer-any-pool) to bypass affinity pinning. Partial recovery within 5 minutes.
- 10:00 UTC: rolled back kernel/libnv on canary nodes; after full rollback, write latency normalized.
- 10:10 UTC: confirmed baseline throughput restored; monitoring returned to nominal by 10:12 UTC.

Root cause (technical):
1) Kernel/libnv regression: the canaried kernel introduced a syscall path regression that increased latency for small, frequent socket writes used by our streaming producer. The regression was workload-specific and only surfaced under streaming I/O patterns.
2) Affinity routing bug: session pinning logic treated transient health-check latency as non-fatal because it relied on average latency. Affinity entries were not invalidated when p95/p99 spiked, causing many sessions to remain routed to the degraded canary nodes.
3) Feedback amplification: pinned sessions experiencing delayed writes triggered client-side reconnect behavior, which increased inbound connection churn and amplified load on the affected nodes, driving queueing and head-of-line blocking.

Why safeguards failed:
- Health-checks used mean latency windows and missed high-percentile degradation.
- Canary rollout lacked a streaming-specific workload test that would have exercised the small-write socket pattern.
- Routing system lacked a fast-path to invalidate affinity on percentile-based health signals.

Immediate mitigations executed:
- Enabled routing fallback (prefer-any-pool) to break affinity hot-pinning (09:42 UTC). This reduced affected sessions from ~18% to ~6% within 5 minutes.
- Scoped rollback of the canaried kernel on implicated nodes (10:0010:10 UTC).
- Temporarily tightened ingress rate limits to reduce reconnect amplification while nodes recovered (09:3010:15 UTC).
- Added expanded logging for streaming socket metrics and affinity table churn (09:50 UTC).

Post-incident actions (short-term):
- Revert the infra kernel/libnv candidate from the rollout artifact store and block re-deployment until mitigations are in place. (Owner: infra)
- Add a p95/p99-based health-check metric to routing health evaluations; iterate on thresholds. (Owner: eng-sre)
- Implement a short TTL invalidation for affinity entries when percentile latency rises above threshold. (Owner: routing service)
- Add a synthetic streaming small-write load test to canary rollout pipeline to catch similar regressions. (Owner: release-engineering)
- Run a dedicated postmortem review with infra and routing teams to agree on rollout gating and observability improvements. (Owner: incident lead)

Longer-term follow-ups (planned):
- Develop an automated affinity invalidation runbook: when p99 exceeds X ms for Y minutes, auto-evacuate affinity to healthy nodes with controlled cutover. (Owner: routing)
- Improve canary release criteria to include workload-shaped e2e tests (streaming small writes, websocket bursts). (Owner: release-engineering)
- Add socket-level tracing to capture per-write syscall timings for future regressions. (Owner: serving-runtime)
- Create a dashboard showing affinity heatmaps and per-pool percentile latency to detect asymmetric patterns earlier. (Owner: observability)

Lessons learned:
- Percentile signals (p95/p99) are critical for streaming workloads; mean-based health checks provide a false sense of safety.
- Routing affinity saves on state rehydration costs but introduces blast radius when health signals are not conservative.
- Canary testing must include representative workload shapes; low-level kernel changes can have surprisingly narrow failure modes.

Runbook changes (to be merged within 72 hours):
- New triage play: if streaming throughput alert triggers and one or two pools show p95/p99 degradation > threshold, immediately verify affinity heatmap and consider enabling prefer-any-pool fallback before manual node restarts.
- Health-check update: include p95 and p99 latency windows; treat high-percentile degradation as a health failure for affinity invalidation.
- Canary gating: require successful streaming small-write synthetic test before kernel/libnv canary proceeds to larger rings.

Action items (owners and due dates):
- infra: block problematic kernel candidate and add canary test; due 2027-10-16.
- routing: implement p95/p99 health-check and affinity TTL; due 2027-10-20.
- release-engineering: add streaming e2e to canary pipeline; due 2027-10-18.
- observability: dashboard and alert refinement for affinity hotspots; due 2027-10-19.
- eng-sre: postmortem write-up and runbook PR; due 2027-10-13.

Appendix (debug notes and artifacts):
- Observable metric snippets: pool-7 write_latency_p50=2ms p95=120ms p99=1250ms at peak; system cpu_iowait spike noted.
- Kernel candidate: libnv-2.14.7-canary (infra-job-321).
- Relevant logs: routing-affinity churn trace ids (trace-9876, trace-9879), socket write syscall traces collected during mitigation window.
- Communication: incident coordination channel Slack thread: ops-incidents/thread-abc123.

Status: in_review. This draft will be updated after the routing and health-check PRs are merged and the infra team confirms the kernel candidate root cause via backtrace correlation.
